verses.1: Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as a negation asking whether one knows with patent clarity—likened to sensory observation—what the Lord did to the Riders of Elephants, rather than whether one literally saw it. The incident occurred in the year of the Prophet’s birth.
verses.2: Al-Mizan identifies their stratagem as the malicious plan to attack Mecca and destroy God’s Sacred House. Taḍlīl, synonymous with iḍlāl, “leading astray,” means that God diverted their efforts so that they missed their goal: they set out to destroy the Kaʿbah but destroyed themselves.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says the birds’ dispersed flocks—abābīl, “separated groups” or “differentiated clusters”—and their hard-clay stones, sijjīl, explain how God rendered the Riders of Elephants’ stratagem futile (105:2).
verses.4: Al-Mizan says the birds’ dispersed flocks—abābīl, “separated groups” or “differentiated clusters”—and their hard-clay stones, sijjīl, explain how God rendered the Riders of Elephants’ stratagem futile (105:2).
verses.5: Al-Mizan glosses ʿaṣf as crop leaves and maʾkūl straw as leaves whose seeds have been eaten, or husks emptied of kernels. It gives two possibilities: after the clay stones struck the Riders they became lifeless bodies, or the stones’ heat burned through their entrails. It also reports the interpretation of worm-blighted, withered leaves, but judges further proposed readings incompatible with Qur’anic language.
